title: Build and Publish Your Portfolio Website with GitHub Pages
text:
Overview
When you apply for a work placement or a graduate role, employers want evidence: what have you built, how did you build it, and can they see it? You probably already have that evidence scattered across many Git repositories - coursework, group projects, hackathon entries, personal experiments. This tutorial shows you how to gather the best of it into a single, professional portfolio website that you own, published free as a static website on GitHub Pages.
You will use Quarto to write your pages in Markdown, render them to plain HTML, and publish them from a GitHub repository. No servers, databases or hosting fees are involved.
crumbs: Build and Publish Your Portfolio Website with GitHub Pages

title: Build and Publish Your Portfolio Website with GitHub Pages
text:
What You’ll Build
By the end of the tutorial you will have a live website at https://<your-username>.github.io containing:

A home page that introduces you and what you’re looking for (placement, graduate role, internship)
A projects page with a card for each showcased project, linking to its GitHub repository and any live demo
Individual project write-ups explaining the problem, your role, the technologies and the outcome
An about / CV page with your skills, education, achievements and contact links
A repeatable workflow for updating the site whenever you finish new work

flowchart LR
  A[Your existing repos] --> B[Plan & select projects]
  B --> C[username.github.io repo]
  C --> D[Quarto pages in Markdown]
  D --> E[Render to docs/]
  E --> F[Push to GitHub]
  F --> G[Live site on GitHub Pages]

Fix the most common problems

title: Build and Publish Your Portfolio Website with GitHub Pages
text:
Who This Is For
Students preparing for a work placement or graduation who already use Git and GitHub for their coursework. You don’t need any web design experience - if you can write a README and run git push, you can complete this tutorial.






TipTime needed



Allow around 4-6 hours in total. Steps 1 and 4 (choosing and writing up your projects) take the longest - and matter the most.
crumbs: Build and Publish Your Portfolio Website with GitHub Pages

title: Prerequisites
text:
Work through this checklist before starting Step 1. Each item takes a few minutes, and having everything ready now saves frustration later.



Basic Git: clone, add, commit, push and pull
Using a terminal (Command Prompt/PowerShell, macOS Terminal or a Linux shell)
Basic Markdown: headings, lists, links and images (a quick reference is enough)





A GitHub account with a professional username. Your username becomes part of your site address (https://<username>.github.io), so if yours is something like xXgamer2004Xx, consider changing it before you start.
Your existing repositories pushed to GitHub. If some projects only live on your laptop or a university GitLab server, push copies to GitHub now (check any academic-integrity rules about publishing coursework first).







Tool
Purpose
Check it works




Git
Version control
git --version


Quarto (1.4 or later)
Builds your site from Markdown
quarto --version


VS Code with the Quarto extension (or RStudio / Positron)
Editing and previewing pages
Open a .qmd file and see syntax highlighting



Run these commands in your terminal:
git --version
quarto --version
git config --global user.name
git config --global user.email
You should see version numbers and your name/email. If user.name or user.email is empty, set them (replace the values in angle brackets with your own details):
git config --global user.name "<Your Name>"
git config --global user.email "<your-email-address>"






ImportantAuthentication



GitHub no longer accepts account passwords for git push. Make sure you can push using either the GitHub CLI (gh auth login), a personal access token, or an SSH key. Test it by pushing a small change to any existing repository.





Create a folder on your computer called portfolio-materials and collect:

A recent, professional photo (optional but recommended)
Your current CV as a PDF
Screenshots or short GIFs of your best projects
Links to your LinkedIn profile and any other professional profiles







Tip



If you’re missing any of the prerequisites, follow the linked installation guides before continuing. The Troubleshooting page covers common installation and authentication problems.

title: Step 3: Build the Site Skeleton
text:
In this step you turn your repository into a Quarto website with Home, Projects and About pages, and preview it on your own computer.




In the root of your <username>.github.io folder, create _quarto.yml:
project:
  type: website
  output-dir: docs

website:
  title: "Alex Jones"
  site-url: "https://<your-username>.github.io"
  description: "Portfolio of Alex Jones - software engineering student"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: projects.qmd
        text: Projects
      - href: about.qmd
        text: About
    right:
      - icon: github
        href: https://github.com/<your-username>
        aria-label: GitHub
      - icon: linkedin
        href: https://www.linkedin.com/in/<your-profile>
        aria-label: LinkedIn
  page-footer:
    center: "Alex Jones. Built with Quarto, hosted on GitHub Pages."

format:
  html:
    theme:
      light: cosmo
      dark: darkly
    toc: false






ImportantWhy output-dir: docs?



Quarto renders your Markdown into HTML in the docs/ folder. In Step 5 you’ll tell GitHub Pages to publish from the docs folder on the main branch. Replace every <your-username> and the example name with your own details.





Create index.qmd. The about template gives you a professional landing page with your photo and links:
---
title: "Alex Jones"
subtitle: "BSc Software Engineering, Year 2"
image: images/profile.jpg
about:
  template: trestles
  links:
    - icon: github
      text: GitHub
      href: https://github.com/<your-username>
    - icon: linkedin
      text: LinkedIn
      href: https://www.linkedin.com/in/<your-profile>
    - icon: envelope
      text: Email
      href: mailto:<your-email-address>
---

I'm a second-year software engineering student interested in back-end
and cloud development. I'm looking for a 12-month placement starting
September 2025.

[See my projects](projects.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}
Copy your photo from portfolio-materials into a new images/ folder as profile.jpg. Paste in the introduction you drafted in Step 1.






Tip



Other about templates include jolla, solana, marquee and broadside. Try a few and pick the one you like - see the Quarto About Pages guide.





Create projects.qmd:
---
title: "Projects"
---

Project listings will go here in Step 4.
Create about.qmd:
---
title: "About Me"
---

## Skills

- **Languages:** Python, Java, JavaScript, SQL
- **Frameworks & tools:** Django, React, Git, Docker

## Education

**BSc (Hons) Software Engineering** - University Name, 2023-2027

## Achievements

- Winner, University Hackathon 2024
- Student Ambassador, 2024-present

## CV

[Download my CV (PDF)](files/cv.pdf)
Copy your CV into a new files/ folder as cv.pdf.



quarto preview
A browser window opens showing your site. Leave quarto preview running - every time you save a file, the page refreshes automatically. Press Ctrl+C in the terminal to stop it.
Your folder should now look like this:
<username>.github.io/
├── _quarto.yml
├── index.qmd
├── projects.qmd
├── about.qmd
├── images/
│   └── profile.jpg
├── files/
│   └── cv.pdf
├── .gitignore
└── README.md



git add .
git commit -m "Add Quarto site skeleton"
git push




Before moving on, verify that:

quarto preview shows your site with a working Home / Projects / About navbar
Your photo, name and introduction appear on the home page
The GitHub and LinkedIn icons link to your profiles
The CV link downloads your PDF





Which setting in _quarto.yml controls where the rendered HTML files are written?




 ✗site-url


 ✓output-dir


 ✗navbar


Clear answer











You created a static site generator project. You write content in Markdown (.qmd), and Quarto converts it into plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Because the output is just static files, GitHub Pages can host it for free with no server-side code.

title: Step 6: Polish and Promote
text:
In this step you make sure the repositories you link to are as professional as your portfolio, check the site for quality and accessibility, and put your link where employers will see it.




A recruiter who clicks View source lands on your repository’s README. For each showcase repository:

README explains what the project is, shows a screenshot, and gives setup/run instructions
About box (cog icon on the repository page) has a one-line description, topic tags and a website link
No secrets: no API keys, passwords or .env files in the code or the history
No clutter: build output, node_modules/, IDE files are covered by .gitignore
Licence added if you’re happy for others to reuse the code







Warning



Deleting a committed secret in a new commit does not remove it from Git history. If you find one, revoke/rotate the key immediately, then consult GitHub’s guide to removing sensitive data.





On your GitHub profile page, click Customize your pins and pin your showcase repositories. Consider adding a profile README (a repository named exactly <your-username>) that links to your portfolio site.



Work through your live site with this checklist:



Check
How




Spelling and grammar
Read every page aloud, or paste text into a spell checker


Broken links
Click every link, or use the W3C Link Checker


Accessibility
Run WAVE or Lighthouse (Chrome DevTools - Lighthouse tab)


Image alt text
Every image has meaningful fig-alt or alt text


Mobile layout
Open the site on your phone; use DevTools device mode


Dark mode
Toggle the light/dark switch and check readability


Personal data
Only share contact details you’re comfortable making public



Aim for a Lighthouse Accessibility score of 90 or above.



In _quarto.yml, make sure site-url and description are set (from Step 3), and add social-sharing previews:
website:
  open-graph: true
  image: images/profile.jpg
This gives your link a title, description and image when shared on LinkedIn, Teams or Slack.



Ask a peer, tutor or careers adviser to spend two minutes on your site and answer:

What role do you think I’m looking for?
Which project impressed you most, and why?
Was anything confusing, broken or missing?

Make changes, then quarto render, commit and push.



Add https://<your-username>.github.io to:

Your CV header, next to your email and LinkedIn
Your LinkedIn profile (Contact info - Website, and the Featured section)
Your GitHub profile bio
Placement and graduate applications that ask for a portfolio or website
Your email signature




Set a reminder at the end of each term to add new projects, update your CV PDF and skills, and remove anything that no longer represents your best work.




Before finishing, verify that:

Every linked repository has a clear README and no exposed secrets
Your showcase repositories are pinned on your GitHub profile
Lighthouse accessibility score is 90+ and there are no broken links
At least one other person has reviewed your site
Your portfolio URL appears on your CV and LinkedIn





You discover an API key in a file that was committed three months ago. What should you do first?




 ✗Delete the file and push a new commit.


 ✓Revoke or rotate the key with the service provider.


 ✗Make the portfolio repository private.


Clear answer











You’ve gone from scattered repositories to a curated, published, professional portfolio - and made sure the code behind it stands up to scrutiny. Congratulations! Head to Troubleshooting if anything isn’t working.

title: Step 2: Create the Pages Repository
text:
In this step you create a special GitHub repository named <username>.github.io and clone it to your computer.






NoteWhy this name?



GitHub gives every account one user site. If a repository is named exactly <your-username>.github.io, its site is published at the root address https://<your-username>.github.io - a short, memorable URL for your CV. Any other repository name is published as a project site at https://<your-username>.github.io/<repo-name>/.







Go to github.com/new.
Owner: your personal account (not an organisation).
Repository name: <your-username>.github.io - for example, if your username is ajones-dev, type ajones-dev.github.io. It must match your username exactly (lowercase is fine).
Visibility: Public. (GitHub Pages on a free account requires a public repository.)
Tick Add a README file.
Click Create repository.

Alternatively, with the GitHub CLI:
gh repo create <your-username>.github.io --public --add-readme



Choose a sensible location (not inside another Git repository) and clone:
cd ~/Documents
git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/<your-username>.github.io.git
cd <your-username>.github.io



Create a file called .gitignore in the repository root with this content:
/.quarto/
*_files/
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db



git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Add .gitignore"
git push
You should see output ending in something like main -> main.






Tip



Refresh the repository page on GitHub - your .gitignore should now appear alongside the README.






Before moving on, verify that:

A public repository named exactly <your-username>.github.io exists on GitHub
You have cloned it locally and your terminal is inside that folder
git push works without errors





Your GitHub username is sam-codes. You create a repository called portfolio. Where will its GitHub Pages site be published?




 ✗https://sam-codes.github.io


 ✓https://sam-codes.github.io/portfolio/


 ✗https://portfolio.github.io


Clear answer











You created the repository that GitHub treats as your personal website. Everything you commit here (in the right folder) will become your public portfolio once Pages is switched on in Step 5.

title: Step 1: Plan Your Portfolio
text:
In this step you audit your existing Git repositories and choose the handful of projects that will tell an employer the most about you.






NoteWhy plan first?



A portfolio is not an archive of everything you’ve done. Recruiters often spend under a minute on a first look. Three to six well-explained projects beat thirty unexplained repository links every time.






If you have the GitHub CLI installed, list your repositories in the terminal:
gh repo list --limit 100
Otherwise, open https://github.com/<your-username>?tab=repositories. Remember to check any organisations you belong to (university modules, group projects, societies) - your best team work may live there.



Copy this table into a document or spreadsheet and fill in one row per repository:












Repository
What it does
Tech used
My role (solo / team)
Shows which skill?
Can be public?
Score (1-5)




weather-app
Mobile weather forecast app
Kotlin, REST API
Solo
API integration, UI
Yes
4


group-cms
Content management system
Django, PostgreSQL
Team of 4 - backend lead
Teamwork, databases
Check with team
5



When scoring, ask yourself:

Relevance - does it match the roles I’m applying for?
Completeness - does it run? Is there a README?
Ownership - can I clearly explain what I contributed?
Story - was there an interesting problem, decision or result?




Pick your highest-scoring projects, aiming for variety: for example, one team project, one solo project, one that shows a different language or domain, and one you did outside of coursework.






WarningAcademic integrity and confidentiality



Before publishing a link to coursework, check your institution’s rules - some assessments must stay private so future students can’t copy them. Never publish code containing client data, API keys or passwords. For group projects, let your teammates know you’re featuring the work.





Write one or two sentences that will become your home-page introduction. Use this template:

I’m a [year/course] student at [institution] interested in [area, e.g. back-end development, data science, UX]. I’m looking for a [placement / graduate role] starting [date].




Your portfolio will have this structure:
flowchart TD
  H[Home] --> P[Projects]
  H --> A[About / CV]
  P --> P1[Project 1 write-up]
  P --> P2[Project 2 write-up]
  P --> P3[Project 3 write-up]




Before moving on, verify that:

You have an audit table covering your repositories (including organisation repos)
You’ve chosen 3-6 showcase projects and checked they can be made public
You’ve written a draft introduction sentence
Your materials (CV, photo, screenshots) are in your portfolio-materials folder





Which of these is the best reason to leave a repository out of your portfolio?




 ✗It was written in a language you don’t use any more.


 ✓It is a current assessment that your institution requires to stay private.


 ✗It was a team project rather than a solo one.


Clear answer











You turned a pile of repositories into a curated selection with a clear purpose. This planning means every page you build in the following steps has a job to do: show a specific employer a specific skill, backed by real code they can inspect.

If you have the GitHub CLI installed, list your repositories in the terminal:
gh repo list --limit 100
Otherwise, open https://github.com/<your-username>?tab=repositories. Remember to check any organisations you belong to (university modules, group projects, societies) - your best team work may live there.



Copy this table into a document or spreadsheet and fill in one row per repository:












Repository
What it does
Tech used
My role (solo / team)
Shows which skill?
Can be public?
Score (1-5)




weather-app
Mobile weather forecast app
Kotlin, REST API
Solo
API integration, UI
Yes
4


group-cms
Content management system
Django, PostgreSQL
Team of 4 - backend lead
Teamwork, databases
Check with team
5



When scoring, ask yourself:

Relevance - does it match the roles I’m applying for?
Completeness - does it run? Is there a README?
Ownership - can I clearly explain what I contributed?
Story - was there an interesting problem, decision or result?




Pick your highest-scoring projects, aiming for variety: for example, one team project, one solo project, one that shows a different language or domain, and one you did outside of coursework.






WarningAcademic integrity and confidentiality



Before publishing a link to coursework, check your institution’s rules - some assessments must stay private so future students can’t copy them. Never publish code containing client data, API keys or passwords. For group projects, let your teammates know you’re featuring the work.





Write one or two sentences that will become your home-page introduction. Use this template:

I’m a [year/course] student at [institution] interested in [area, e.g. back-end development, data science, UX]. I’m looking for a [placement / graduate role] starting [date].




Your portfolio will have this structure:
flowchart TD
  H[Home] --> P[Projects]
  H --> A[About / CV]
  P --> P1[Project 1 write-up]
  P --> P2[Project 2 write-up]
  P --> P3[Project 3 write-up]




Before moving on, verify that:

You have an audit table covering your repositories (including organisation repos)
You’ve chosen 3-6 showcase projects and checked they can be made public
You’ve written a draft introduction sentence
Your materials (CV, photo, screenshots) are in your portfolio-materials folder





Which of these is the best reason to leave a repository out of your portfolio?




 ✗It was written in a language you don’t use any more.


 ✓It is a current assessment that your institution requires to stay private.


 ✗It was a team project rather than a solo one.


Clear answer











You turned a pile of repositories into a curated selection with a clear purpose. This planning means every page you build in the following steps has a job to do: show a specific employer a specific skill, backed by real code they can inspect.

title: Step 5: Publish to GitHub Pages
text:
In this step you render your site to static HTML, push it to GitHub and switch on GitHub Pages so your portfolio is live on the web.
flowchart LR
  A[Edit .qmd files] --> B[quarto render]
  B --> C[HTML in docs/]
  C --> D[git commit & push]
  D --> E[GitHub Pages serves docs/]




GitHub Pages runs a tool called Jekyll by default, which can hide files and folders starting with _. Quarto’s output doesn’t need Jekyll, so turn it off by creating an empty file:
touch .nojekyll
On Windows PowerShell use New-Item .nojekyll -ItemType File. (Quarto also adds .nojekyll inside docs/ automatically when rendering - keeping one in the root does no harm.)



Stop quarto preview if it’s running (Ctrl+C), then run:
quarto render
You should see each page listed as it is rendered, followed by Output created: docs/index.html. Open the docs/ folder - it contains plain HTML, CSS, images and your CV.






Important



quarto preview does not reliably update docs/ for every page. Always run a full quarto render before you commit.





git add .
git commit -m "Render site for publishing"
git push




Open your repository on GitHub and click Settings.
In the left sidebar choose Pages.
Under Build and deployment, set Source to Deploy from a branch.
Set Branch to main and the folder to /docs.
Click Save.




Click the Actions tab. You’ll see a workflow called pages build and deployment. When it shows a green tick (usually under two minutes), visit:
https://<your-username>.github.io
Your portfolio is live!






Tip



Add the URL to your repository’s About box on GitHub (the cog icon next to About on the repository home page) so visitors can find the live site.





From now on, every time you change your site:
quarto render
git add .
git commit -m "Describe your change"
git push
GitHub Pages redeploys automatically within a minute or two.






NoteOptional: publish with quarto publish instead





Quarto can manage a separate gh-pages branch for you. Remove output-dir: docs from _quarto.yml, add /_site/ to .gitignore, then run quarto publish gh-pages. In Settings - Pages select the gh-pages branch and / (root). This keeps rendered HTML out of your main branch, but you must remember to run the publish command after each change. See the Quarto GitHub Pages guide.







Before moving on, verify that:

https://<your-username>.github.io loads your home page
The navbar, project cards and CV download all work on the live site
Images display (not broken icons)
The site loads on your phone as well as your laptop





You edited about.qmd, committed and pushed, but the live site hasn’t changed after ten minutes. What is the most likely cause?




 ✓You didn’t run quarto render, so the HTML in docs/ is still the old version.


 ✗GitHub Pages only updates once a day.


 ✗The repository needs to be made private.


Clear answer











You published a static website: GitHub Pages simply serves the files in your docs/ folder to anyone who visits your URL. There’s no server code to maintain, no hosting cost, and every version of your site is recorded in Git history.

title: Step 4: Showcase Your Projects
text:
In this step you write a page for each showcase project, linking to its Git repository, and generate a Projects page that lists them automatically as cards.




Inside your <username>.github.io repository:
mkdir -p projects/weather-app projects/group-cms
Use short, lowercase, hyphenated names - they become part of the URL (e.g. https://<username>.github.io/projects/weather-app/).



Create projects/weather-app/index.qmd and copy in a screenshot as projects/weather-app/screenshot.png:
---
title: "Weather Forecast App"
description: "An Android app that shows 7-day forecasts using the Open-Meteo API."
date: 2024-05-01
image: screenshot.png
categories: [Kotlin, Android, REST API, Solo]
---

[View source on GitHub](https://github.com/<your-username>/weather-app){.btn .btn-primary}
[Live demo](https://<your-username>.github.io/weather-app/){.btn .btn-outline-secondary}

![The forecast screen showing a 7-day outlook](screenshot.png){fig-alt="Phone screen with a list of seven days, each with a weather icon and temperatures"}

## The problem

What need or question did the project address? Who was it for?

## My role

Solo project / team of four - I was responsible for ...

## How I built it

Key technologies, architecture and one or two interesting decisions.
A short code snippet can help:

```kotlin
val forecast = api.getForecast(lat, lon, days = 7)
```

## Outcome

What worked? Grade, users, performance, feedback, awards?

## What I learned

One or two honest reflections - employers value these.






TipWrite for a recruiter, not a marker



Use the Problem - Role - Approach - Outcome - Learning structure. Lead with results, keep paragraphs short, and be specific about your contribution in team projects (“I designed the database schema and wrote the REST API” beats “we built a CMS”).


Repeat for each of the 3-6 projects you chose in Step 1.



Replace the contents of projects.qmd with:
---
title: "Projects"
listing:
  contents: projects
  type: grid
  sort: "date desc"
  categories: true
  fields: [image, title, description, categories]
---

A selection of projects from my studies and spare time.
Each card links to a write-up with source code and demos.
Quarto scans the projects/ folder, reads each page’s front matter and builds a grid of cards with filterable category tags - you never have to edit the list by hand.



You don’t need a write-up for every repository. Add a short section to the bottom of projects.qmd for honourable mentions:
## More on GitHub

- [algorithms-practice](https://github.com/<your-username>/algorithms-practice) - solutions to data-structures exercises in Java
- [dotfiles](https://github.com/<your-username>/dotfiles) - my development environment setup
- [All repositories](https://github.com/<your-username>?tab=repositories)



Add a short “Featured work” listing below your introduction in index.qmd:
## Featured work

::: {#featured}
:::
and add this to the index.qmd front matter:
listing:
  id: featured
  contents: projects
  type: grid
  max-items: 3
  sort: "date desc"



quarto preview
Check every card, link and image, then:
git add .
git commit -m "Add project showcase pages"
git push




Before moving on, verify that:

Each showcase project has its own page with a screenshot and alt text
Every project page links to its GitHub repository (and live demo if it has one)
The Projects page shows a grid of cards with working category filters
Team projects clearly state your personal contribution





You add a new project folder with an index.qmd. What do you need to change in projects.qmd for it to appear as a card?




 ✗Add a new link to the list in projects.qmd.


 ✗Add the project to the navbar in _quarto.yml.


 ✓Nothing - the listing finds pages in the projects/ folder automatically.


Clear answer











You connected your portfolio to the evidence behind it. Each write-up gives a recruiter the story, while the repository link lets a technical interviewer inspect the code. Using a listing means adding future projects takes minutes.
